notes.title: Process vs Thread
notes.body:
A **process** has its own memory space; a **thread** shares memory with other threads in the same process.

- Context-switching threads is cheaper than processes (no address-space switch).
- Threads need explicit synchronization (locks, semaphores) since they share memory.
- Common interview probe: *what breaks if two threads increment the same counter without a lock?*

notes.title: Deadlock: the Four Conditions
notes.body:
A deadlock requires all four of: **mutual exclusion**, **hold and wait**, **no preemption**, **circular wait**. Breaking any one prevents it.

- Prevention: acquire locks in a fixed global order (breaks circular wait).
- Detection: resource-allocation graph cycle detection.
- A classic interview trap: *'our deadlock only happens under negative/variable timing'* — tests whether you understand it's a race, not a deterministic bug.

notes.title: Virtual Memory & Paging
notes.body:
Each process sees a contiguous virtual address space; the OS maps virtual pages to physical frames via a **page table**.

- A **page fault** occurs when a referenced page isn't in physical memory.
- Thrashing: when the working set exceeds available RAM, causing constant paging and collapsing throughput.
- TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) caches recent translations to avoid a page-table walk on every memory access.

notes.title: Scheduling Algorithms
notes.body:
- **FCFS**: simple, can cause convoy effect.
- **SJF**: optimal average wait time, but needs to know burst length (often estimated).
- **Round Robin**: fair, time-sliced; quantum size trades off responsiveness vs context-switch overhead.
- **Priority scheduling**: risk of starvation, mitigated by aging.

notes.title: ACID Properties
notes.body:
**Atomicity** (all-or-nothing), **Consistency** (valid state to valid state), **Isolation** (concurrent transactions don't interfere), **Durability** (committed survives a crash).

- Isolation is the one with real trade-offs: serializable is safest and slowest; read-committed is common and allows some anomalies.

notes.title: Normalization (1NF → 3NF)
notes.body:
- **1NF**: atomic columns, no repeating groups.
- **2NF**: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key.
- **3NF**: 2NF + no transitive dependency (non-key columns depend only on the key).

Normalizing reduces update anomalies but can increase the number of joins needed — denormalization is a deliberate trade for read performance.

notes.title: Indexes: B-Tree vs Hash
notes.body:
A **B-Tree index** supports range queries and ordering (`WHERE x > 5`, `ORDER BY`); a **hash index** supports only equality lookups but is O(1) average.

- Most relational databases default to B-Tree indexes because range queries are common.
- An index on a low-cardinality column (e.g. boolean) often doesn't help — the optimizer may ignore it.

notes.title: Isolation Levels & Anomalies
notes.body:
- **Read Uncommitted**: dirty reads possible.
- **Read Committed**: no dirty reads, but non-repeatable reads possible.
- **Repeatable Read**: no non-repeatable reads, but phantom reads possible (in some engines).
- **Serializable**: no anomalies, but lowest concurrency.

Interview probe: *given this isolation level, what could go wrong with two concurrent transfers between the same two accounts?*

notes.title: TCP vs UDP
notes.body:
**TCP**: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, flow/congestion controlled — at the cost of latency (handshake, retransmits).
**UDP**: connectionless, no ordering/reliability guarantees — lower latency, used where an app can tolerate loss (video calls, DNS, gaming).

notes.title: The Three-Way Handshake
notes.body:
SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK establishes a TCP connection, synchronizing initial sequence numbers both ways.

- A SYN flood (sending SYNs and never completing the handshake) exhausts the server's half-open connection table — a classic DoS vector mitigated by SYN cookies.

notes.title: DNS Resolution Path
notes.body: Browser cache → OS cache → recursive resolver → root server → TLD server → authoritative server. Each step is cached with a TTL, which is why DNS changes don't propagate instantly.

notes.title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2
notes.body: HTTP/1.1 opens multiple connections to work around head-of-line blocking from one request blocking the next. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection, with header compression — but head-of-line blocking can still occur at the TCP layer if a packet is lost (addressed by QUIC/HTTP3, which runs over UDP).

notes.title: The Four Pillars
notes.body: **Encapsulation** (hide internal state), **Abstraction** (expose only what's needed), **Inheritance** (reuse via an is-a relationship), **Polymorphism** (one interface, many implementations).

notes.title: Composition over Inheritance
notes.body: Inheritance creates tight coupling to a parent's implementation and can break with deep hierarchies (the fragile base class problem). Composition ("has-a") is often more flexible: build behavior by combining small, swappable objects rather than extending a class.

notes.title: SOLID Principles
notes.body:
- **S**ingle Responsibility
- **O**pen/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification)
- **L**iskov Substitution (a subtype must be substitutable for its base type)
- **I**nterface Segregation (many small interfaces over one large one)
- **D**ependency Inversion (depend on abstractions, not concretions)

notes.title: Common Design Patterns
notes.body:
- **Singleton**: one instance, global access point (watch for hidden global state / testability issues).
- **Factory**: delegate object creation to a method, decoupling the caller from concrete classes.
- **Observer**: subscribers get notified of changes in a subject (pub/sub is this pattern distributed).
- **Strategy**: swap an algorithm's implementation at runtime behind a common interface.

notes.title: The Memory Hierarchy
notes.body: Registers → L1/L2/L3 cache → RAM → SSD/disk, each level trading capacity for speed. A program with good **locality of reference** (temporal and spatial) runs much faster because it hits the fast, small levels more often.

notes.title: Cache Lines & False Sharing
notes.body: CPUs fetch memory in fixed-size cache lines (commonly 64 bytes). If two threads on different cores modify different variables that happen to sit on the same cache line, the cache-coherence protocol bounces the line between cores — **false sharing** — silently destroying performance despite no logical data race.

notes.title: Pipelining & Branch Prediction
notes.body: Instruction pipelining overlaps fetch/decode/execute/writeback stages across instructions. A mispredicted branch flushes the pipeline, costing cycles — which is why tight, predictable loops are often faster than code with many unpredictable branches.

notes.title: Instruction Set Basics: CISC vs RISC
notes.body: **CISC** (e.g. x86): fewer, more complex instructions, variable length. **RISC** (e.g. ARM): simpler, fixed-length instructions, more registers, designed for efficient pipelining — a major reason ARM chips are power-efficient.
